content: In 2016, the Ghana Health Services established an intersectoral WASH (Water, Sanitation, and Hygiene) technical working group and expanded its Infection Prevention and Control (IPC) program to include WASH. This working group developed a national WASH guide for healthcare facilities, which included detailed indicators, standards, operational and maintenance procedures, and cleaning protocols. They piloted several approaches to improve services, including the use of the WASH FIT tool. By 2018, the group had developed and costed a national strategy for WASH in healthcare facilities, aligning it with Sustainable Development Goals (SDG) 3 (universal access to healthcare) and SDG 6 (clean water and sanitation). The strategy also included a plan to finance most improvements using domestic resources. A 2011 costing study in 117 rural Kenyan healthcare facilities demonstrated that introducing low-cost, portable handwashing and drinking water stations, combined with health worker training and visual WASH guides, was an affordable and effective shortto medium-term solution to reduce healthcare-associated infections. These interventions were quickly implemented and served as valuable interim solutions while more sustainable WASH services were being planned and constructed. In Liberia, the 2014–2016 West Africa Ebola outbreak highlighted the critical need for improved WASH services in healthcare facilities. In 2016, Liberia’s Vice President launched a minimum WASH package, including new WASH standards and the adoption of WASH FIT as the national implementation tool. District Health Teams assumed responsibility for regular supervision and mentoring, working with a national WASH FIT team composed of government and partner trainers. As a result, WASH is now prioritized in quality and health security strategies, and all healthcare facilities in Liberia implement WASH FIT improvement plans. However, limited governance and insufficient funding constrain the ability to conduct frequent supportive supervision visits. In Tajikistan, the Ministry of Health and Social Protection (MHSP) began piloting WASH FIT in selected healthcare facilities in 2018. This initiative was introduced during a national roundtable on WASH in healthcare facilities, which included key stakeholders. Specific WASH targets were set and aligned with WHO and UNECE protocols. The MHSP took the lead in integrating WASH requirements into existing and developing policies and standards, with improved collaboration from partners like Oxfam. However, outdated infrastructure and reliance on a few committed individuals remain challenges. In Sierra Leone, the Ministry of Health and Sanitation (MOHS) recognized the need to improve healthcare waste management systems following the Ebola epidemic. Building on the 2015 National IPC Guidelines, the MOHS published National WASH Standards and Guidelines for Healthcare Facilities in 2017. These guidelines specified waste treatment models for each tier of the healthcare system. When issues arose with the standard incinerator models, local engineers made design modifications using locally available materials to create context-specific solutions. Innovative and environmentally friendly approaches to WASH have been adopted in resource-scarce environments. These include low-cost water-treatment devices, such as large-membrane filters and electro-chlorinators for on-site chlorine production, as well as locally produced hand rubs and simple handwashing stations. Environmentally friendly energy solutions, such as biodigesters and solar arrays, have also been implemented to power WASH-related equipment and provide hot water and lighting. Rainwater harvesting and regular monitoring of plumbing systems for leaks ensure efficient water use.
